Source: https://eclypsium.com/blog/linux-malware-fake-kernel-threads/
Saved evidence: /usr/local/var/cyclotron/tmp.noindex/cyclotron-98e79cc7/scratch/threat-feed/3952/article.txt
The saved text names a Rust implant running as [kworker/u:8:0], a Go agent
running as [kworker/7:2], and scheduled relaunch through cron. These are
concrete named-family behaviors and exact process-name artifacts, despite
the saved article's roundup-like format. The source URL returned HTTP 403;
its image/code content could not be independently recovered. Saved text
contains no images and one defensive ps command; extraction is recorded in
article-images.json and article-code.txt outside the sample directory.

Primary context: https://sansec.io/research/stylesmuggler-0day
Downloaded HTML, extracted code/image/link inventory, the report illustration,
and original IOC block are preserved beside article.txt. The illustration is
a conceptual graphic with no code, commands, or technical indicators. The primary report specifies the
*/5 cron command and ~/.local/share/.gvfsd/gvfsd-user path for the early build;
the twice-hourly 13,43 schedule belongs to the later fc-cache variant. The
saved summary compresses those variants. No CVE/exploit rules were invented;
CVE-2026-20349 is a feed-only indicator absent from the saved text.

Samples are source reconstructions, not original recovered malware. They
implement only userspace name spoofing and cron relaunch. C and Rust use the
Linux PR_SET_NAME operation; Python translates the title technique to the
real setproctitle API. The Rust sample combines the observed OpenCart worker
name with the primary report's cron mechanism as a synthetic language/name
variant. The sources are never executed. Network tasking, exploitation,
Tengu-specific init/procd setup, and Cyclops Blink identity are not inferred
from missing implementation evidence. Linux-kernel specificity (including OpenWrt/Android title APIs) is intentional:
these kernel-thread names have no equivalent meaning on Windows/macOS.

New observations require actual call nodes or call arguments. They accept
numeric PR_SET_NAME, qualified Rust APIs, Python import aliases, and other
kernel-thread names through real title APIs. Cron persistence requires the
renaming action, a complete recurring schedule, cron spool path, and a file
write within 20 lines. It has no campaign path, C2, hash, or filename gate.
The Node title implementation is reused as an alternative, not duplicated.

Retired source-prctl-kworker-masquerade: its unbound name+opcode co-occurrence
could convict diagnostic/comment text; the new action matcher replaces it
at suspicious, with hostile reserved for the cron-persistence combination.
Consolidated the metadata source-kworker-name-literal into the canonical
process/info/name bracketed-name reference; its two remaining consumers now
require bracketed names. Bare kworker source names no longer satisfy those
two objectives. Exact and ancestor name-reference consumers were audited;
most are ELF-only, and the source extensions retain an actual name observation.
The full name leaf already contains 100 rules, so no additional name atom was
added. Existing name references are notable, not declarations of spoofing.

Rust fs::write now uses parsed call evidence and reports neutral writes even
inside test directories. The text matcher and path/test exclusions suppressed
real calls and could match comments. Existing exact consumers remain unchanged;
focused controls exercise both normal writes and comment-only examples.

Benign controls and API variants live in cleave's tests/fixtures directory.
Run the focused cases with python3 testdata/taxonomy/fake-kernel-thread-titles/check.py. Feed samples remain in the requested scratch testdata.
All three feed samples passed their first completed scan at the suspicious
floor; subsequent rule edits fix precision, placement, and Rust write coverage.
Initial rule-load errors produced no sample verdict and are not floor tests.

Identity inventory: the saved summary names no hashes or network endpoints.
SHA256 and ENDPOINTS additionally preserve the primary Sansec report's
malicious/suspicious identities with their roles in sansec-iocs.txt. These
include separate attacker toolchains and the exact callback hostname; shared
relay IPs and the compromised incofar host are suspicious in this chain and
do not imply their providers or all hosted content are malicious. The source
CIDR is a reported source range, not an assertion that every address attacked.
Template exfil hostnames remain in notes rather than being invented as exact
endpoints. Public IP-lookup services, vendor/source sites, sample email fields,
and the clean Adminer binary hash are excluded. BuildID b183335f5474b15df95c48ca781e75c27e704ac2
and the X-Cache-Token value are not file hashes. No package identity/version is
implicated: PURLS is empty. No source-package PURL is inferred from binaries.

Final focused verification: 17 cases passed. Final atomscan scan: C and Rust
each have 1 hostile + 2 suspicious findings; Python has 1 hostile + 1 suspicious.
The required floor is met for all three suspicious-tier samples. Full facts
(including decoded string literals), final scan reports, and verification.json
are retained beside article.txt. Atomscan exits 1 for flagged samples.
